title: Privileged Account Management
summary: Privileged account management is the discipline of limiting, controlling, and monitoring the accounts and roles that can change security-relevant configuration, access sensitive data, or administer other systems. Real implementations combine several mechanisms: a tiered administrative model that separates directory, server, and workstation administration so that no single credential can cross tiers, dedicated administrative accounts that are never used for mail or browsing, credential vaulting with automatic rotation for shared and service accounts, just-in-time elevation that grants a role for a bounded window with approval and full session recording, and the removal of standing local administrator rights from standard user workstations. The control removes the two conditions attackers rely on most: reusable credentials with broad reach, and quiet elevation paths that leave no approval trail. It breaks behaviours including account discovery and enumeration of privileged groups, credential access through cached secrets and process memory on administrative workstations, exploitation of elevation control mechanisms such as user account control misconfiguration and setuid binaries, and the use of remote services to move laterally with administrative shares. It also directly constrains impact, because destructive actions such as recovery inhibition and mass encryption require privileged reach that a tightly brokered model does not grant by default. Honest limitations are mostly organisational. Tiered models collapse when administrators reuse a single identity across tiers because it is convenient, and vaulting is defeated if the vault becomes a single unmonitored credential store reachable from the same flat network as everything else. Just-in-time access fails when approval becomes a rubber stamp or when emergency break-glass accounts retain permanent standing privilege. Service accounts remain the hardest case, because they cannot always be rotated without an outage and are frequently excluded from management scope. Failure modes include allowing interactive logon for service identities, leaving former administrators in privileged groups, permitting administrative sessions from ordinary workstations, and never reviewing who actually used the privilege that was granted.
objectives: Explain how a tiered administrative model is designed and how credential reuse across tiers defeats it.
Describe how credential vaulting, rotation, and just-in-time elevation are implemented and where they typically break down.
Identify the privileged account and elevation control weaknesses that most often enable privilege escalation in practice.
Explain how removing standing local administrator rights changes attacker options on workstations.
Describe how service and machine accounts should be scoped, monitored, and rotated without causing outages.
Explain how session recording and approval trails turn privileged access management into a detection source.
Evaluate a privileged access estate, including break-glass accounts, and recommend a remediation sequence.
